{{short description|Species of plant}} {{Lead too short|date=January 2021}} {{speciesbox | name = Tomatillo | image = Tomatillo.jpg | image_caption = Tomatillos | genus = Physalis | species = philadelphica | authority = [[Jean-Baptiste Lamarck|Lam.]] (1786) | synonyms = ''Physalis ixocarpa'' Brot. }} [[File:Physalis ixocarpa MHNT.BOT.2008.1.52.jpg|thumb|''Physalis ixocarpa'' – [[MHNT]]]] The '''tomatillo''' (''Physalis philadelphica'' and ''Physalis ixocarpa''), also known as the '''Mexican husk tomato''', is a plant of the [[nightshade]] family bearing small, spherical, and green or green-purple fruit.{{cite book|last=Morton|first=Julia F|authorlink=Julia Morton|chapter=Mexican husk tomato, ''Physalis ixocarpa'' Brot., ''Physalis aequata'' Jacq. |title= Fruits of Warm Climates|chapter-url=http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/morton/mexican_husk_tomato.html|year=1987|publisher=New Crop Resource Online Program, Center for New Crops and Plant Products, Purdue University|location= W. Lafayette, IN|isbn=978-0-9610184-1-2|pages=434–7}} Tomatillos originated in [[Mexico]] and were cultivated in the [[Pre-Columbian Mexico|pre-Columbian era]].{{cite book |last=Metcalfe de Plata |first=Edith |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QhLut4HCclsC&pg=PA17 |title=Mexican Vegetarian Cooking |publisher=Inner Traditions/Bear |year=1984 |isbn=978-0-89281-341-4 |page=17}} A staple of [[Mexican cuisine]], they are eaten both raw and cooked in a variety of dishes, notably [[salsa verde]]. The tomatillo is a [[perennial plant]], but is generally grown for agriculture each year as if it were an [[annual plant|annual]]. == Names == The tomatillo (from [[Nahuatl]], ''{{linktext|tomatl}}'') is also known as husk tomato,{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HoDXp_jP1MwC&pg=PT249|title=Fresh Mexico: 100 Simple Recipes for True Mexican Flavor|last=Valladolid|first=Marcela|publisher=Potter/TenSpeed/Harmony|year=2010|isbn=978-0-307-88553-1|page=249}} Mexican groundcherry,{{PLANTS|id=PHPH2|taxon=Physalis philadelphica|access-date=31 January 2016}} large-flowered tomatillo,{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}} or Mexican husk tomato. Some of these names, however, can also refer to other species in the genus ''[[Physalis]]''. Other names are Mexican green tomato and miltomate. In [[Spanish language|Spanish]], it is called ''tomate de cáscara'' (husk tomato), ''tomate de fresadilla'' (little strawberry tomato), ''tomate milpero'' (field tomato), ''tomate verde'' (green tomato), ''tomatillo'' (Mexico; this term means "little [[tomato]]" elsewhere), ''miltomate'' (Mexico, [[Guatemala]]), ''farolito'' (little lantern), or simply ''tomate'' (in which case the tomato is called ''jitomate'' from Nahuatl {{linktext|xitomatl}}). The tomatillo genus name ''Physalis'' is from New Latin ''physalis'', coined by Linnaeus from Ancient Greek φυσαλλίς (''physallís'', "bladder, wind instrument"), itself from φυσιόω (''physióō'', "to puff up, blow up"), {{linktext|φυσώ}} (physṓ).{{citation needed|date=October 2020}} Ixocarpa means "slimy fruit", referencing a sticky or slimy coat often on a tomatillo before it ruptures from the [[Sepal|calyx]].{{Cite web |title=ixo- |url=https://www.mushroomthejournal.com/greatlakesdata/Terms/ixo472.html |access-date=2024-01-07 |website=www.mushroomthejournal.com}} == Distribution == Tomatillos are native to [[Central America]] and [[Mexico]], having a wild growth range from Mexico to [[Costa Rica]].{{Cite journal |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0968089621001036|title = Withanolides from dietary tomatillo suppress HT1080 cancer cell growth by targeting mutant IDH1| date=2021 | doi=10.1016/j.bmc.2021.116095 | last1=Yang | first1=Yueying | last2=Xiang | first2=Ke | last3=Sun | first3=Dejuan | last4=Zheng | first4=Mengzhu | last5=Song | first5=Zhuorui | last6=Li | first6=Mingxue | last7=Wang | first7=Xuanbin | last8=Li | first8=Hua | last9=Chen | first9=Lixia | journal=Bioorganic & Medicinal Chemistry | volume=36 | pmid=33735687 | url-access=subscription }}{{Cite web |url=https://www.growables.org/informationVeg/TomatilloAdvCropPurdue.htm|title = Tomatillo: A Potential Vegetable Crop for Louisiana}}Jiménez-Santana et al., 2012 The plant is grown mostly in the Mexican states of [[Hidalgo (state)|Hidalgo]] and [[Morelos]], and in the highlands of [[Guatemala]] where it is known as ''miltomate''. In the United States, tomatillos have been cultivated since 1863, with one dubbed "jamberry" in 1945 and others with the names "Mayan husk tomato" and "jumbo husk tomato". Further distribution occurred in the [[Bahamas]], [[Puerto Rico]], [[Jamaica]], and [[Florida]]. By the middle of the 20th century, the plant was further exported to [[India]], [[Australia]], [[South Africa]], and [[Kenya]]. The wild tomatillo and related plants are found everywhere in the Americas except in the far north, with the highest diversity in Mexico. In 2017, scientists reported on their discovery and analysis of ''[[Physalis infinemundi]]'', a fossil ''Physalis'' found in the [[Patagonia]]n region of Argentina, dated to 52 million years [[Before Present|BP]]. The finding has pushed back the earliest appearance of the [[Solanaceae]] plant family and the ''Physalis'' genus of which the tomatillo is a part.{{cite journal | doi = 10.1126/science.aag2737 | pmid=28059765 | volume=355 | issue=6320 | title=Eocene lantern fruits from Gondwanan Patagonia and the early origins of Solanaceae | year=2017 | journal=Science | pages=71–75 | last1 = Wilf | first1 = Peter | last2 = Carvalho | first2 = Mónica R. | last3 = Gandolfo | first3 = María A. | last4 = Cúneo | first4 = N. Rubén| bibcode=2017Sci...355...71W | s2cid=206651318 }} == Cultivation == === History === [[File:Physalis ixocarpa.JPG|thumb|right|Purple tomatillos (''Physalis ixocarpa'')]] [[File:Tomatillo 01 cropped.jpg|thumb|right|Green tomatillos (''Physalis philadelphica'')]] Tomatillos were domesticated in Mexico before the coming of Europeans and played an important part in the culture of the [[Maya civilization|Maya]] and the [[Aztec]]s, more important than the [[tomato]].{{cite book|last=Small|first=Ernest|title=Top 100 Exotic Food Plants|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Au3RBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA118|year=2011|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=978-1-4398-5688-8|pages=117–20}} The [[species|specific name]] ''philadelphica'' dates to the 18th century.{{failed verification|date=December 2021}} === Production === There is limited information about tomatillo production,{{Cite journal|last=Diaz-Perez J., Phatak S.C., Giddings D., Bertrand D., Mills H.A.|date=2015|title=Root zone temperature, plant growth and fruit yield of tomatillo as affected by plastic film mulch|journal=HortScience|volume=40|issue=5|pages=1312–1319|doi=10.21273/HORTSCI.40.5.1312|doi-access=free}} even though tomatillos are distributed and grown worldwide as a home-grown garden plant. Tomatillos are mainly cultivated in outdoor fields in [[Mexico]] and [[Guatemala]] on a large scale. Smaller crops are planted in many parts of the United States.{{Cite journal|last=Smith R., Jimenez M., Cantwell M.|date=1999|title=Tomatillo production in California|url=http://anrcatalog.ucanr.edu/pdf/7246.pdf|journal=University of California - Agriculture and Natural Resources}} In Mexico, tomatillos are planted within a wide range of altitudes. ===Soil and climate requirements=== In general, tomatillo plants are tolerant of many different soil conditions. However, they do best in well-drained, sandy, fertile soil conditions with a [[pH]] between 5.5 and 7.3.{{Cite book|title=Easy gardening for Texas|last=Masabni J|publisher=Texas A&M University Press|year=2016|isbn=978-0972104975}} Tomatillo plants are [[Cold sensitivity|cold sensitive]].{{Cite journal|last=Eldon E., Cynthia H., Richard J.|date=2003|title=Tomatillos|url=https://store.extension.iastate.edu/Product/Tomatillos|journal=Iowa State University - Extension Store}} They grow best at {{convert|25|to|32|C|F}}. Below {{convert|16|C|F}}, growth is very poor. Tomatillo plants prefer full sun exposure and warm locations.{{Cite web|url=https://www.mein-schoener-garten.de/pflanzen/gemuese/tomatillo-13926|title=Tomatillos|website=Mein schöner Garten}} ===Seedbed requirement and sowing=== Transplanting is the most common practice for planting tomatillo plants. Transplants are produced in greenhouses or transplant beds.{{Cite web|url=http://www.omafra.gov.on.ca/CropOp/en/spec_veg/fruit_veg/toma.html|title=Tomatillo|date=2012|website=Speciality cropportunity}} Germination occurs at {{convert|20|to|27|C|F}}. Transplanting occurs 6 to 8 weeks after seeding and when the risk of frost is past. Transplants produced indoors need to harden off in a warm, sunny place for a few days before being planted outside. Direct outdoor seeding can only be done if no frost risk exists and soil temperature is higher than {{convert|15|C|F}}. Direct outdoor seeding leads to the shortening of the vegetation period. Due to its branching growing pattern, a single plant requires sufficient growing space. Tomatillos are typically grown in rows {{convert|0.7|to|1.6|m|ftin|0|abbr=on}} apart. Although tomatillo is a [[perennial plant]], overwintering is difficult, so it is normally cultivated as an annual plant. ===Fertilization and field management=== Tomatillo plants can reach heights of {{convert|1.5|to|2|m|ft|frac=2|sp=us}}.{{citation needed|date=December 2019}} Due to their rapid and branching growth, it is recommended to stake them. Staking also facilitates later harvesting and prevents the fruit from touching the ground, which reduces damage to fruit and husk. Staking can also reduce disease and slug damage. Fertilization is recommended at a moderate level. An application of {{convert|40|-|90|kg/ha|abbr=on}} of [[phosphorus]] is common. Other nutrients and fertilizers (N/ K) may be required depending on soil type and irrigation. For non-commercial production, regular fertilization is recommended. Although tomatillo plants become more drought-tolerant as they age, regular watering is required. Tomatillo plants require {{convert|25|-|38|mm|in|frac=8|abbr=on}} of water per week. Water can come from rainfall or irrigation. Irrigation can be managed by drip, sprinkler, furrow, or watering can. Irrigation frequency depends on weather and the crop's growth stage, ranging from once or twice a week to daily during hot weather. Weeds are a serious challenge in tomatillo production and are especially important during the first few weeks. Plastic and organic mulches help to control weeds effectively. Applications of plastic mulches also help to restrict soil water evaporation and modify [[microclimate]], thereby affecting tomatillo growth and yield. ===Harvest and postharvest treatment=== Tomatillos are harvested when the fruits fill the calyx. This state is normally achieved 65 to 100 days after transplanting. Fruit production continues for 1 to 2 months or until the first frost. Harvesting occurs regularly, typically every day, and is done by hand. A plant produces 60 to 200 fruits within a single growing season, with an average yield of about {{convert|9|ST/acre|t/ha|order=flip|abbr=off}}. Tomatillos can be stored for up to three weeks in a cold and humid environment. ==Culinary uses == Tomatillos can be harvested at different stages of ripeness. For ''[[salsa verde]]'', harvesting may be done early when the fruit is sour with a light flavor. Tomatillos can be picked later when the fruits are seedier for a sweeter taste.{{cite web|last1=Johansen|first1=Kristen|title=Tomatillos: Fruits with benefits|url=http://www.roanoke.com/life/down_to_earth/tomatillos-fruits-with-benefits/article_860acb78-8bab-58c3-8da3-37b6d203c87d.html|website=The Roanoke Times|date=15 July 2011 |access-date=October 17, 2017}} Tomatillos have diverse uses in stews, soups, salads, [[curry|curries]], [[stirfry|stirfries]], baking, cooking with meats, [[marmalade]], and desserts. Tomatillos are a key ingredient in fresh and cooked Mexican and Central-American [[green sauce]]s. The green color and tart flavor are the main culinary contributions of the fruit. Purple and red-ripening cultivars often have a slight sweetness, unlike the green- and yellow-ripening cultivars, so they generally are used in jams and preserves. Like their close relative, the [[Physalis peruviana|Cape gooseberry]], tomatillos have a high [[pectin]] content. Another characteristic is that they tend to have a varying degree of a sappy, sticky coating, mostly when used on the green side out of the husk. Ripe tomatillos keep refrigerated for about two weeks. They keep longer with the husks removed and the fruit refrigerated in sealed plastic bags.{{cite news|url=http://www.latimes.com/features/food/la-fo-tomatillo14-2008may14,0,1107342.story|title=Tomatillo: a green sourpuss with a sweet side|date=14 May 2008|last2=Deane|first2=Donna|newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]]|access-date=3 August 2009|first1=Noelle|last1=Carter}} They may also be frozen whole or sliced. Tomatillos can also be dried to enhance the sweetness of the fruit in a way similar to dried [[Cranberry|cranberries]], with a hint of tomato flavor.{{cite journal|last1=Kindscher|first1=K.|last2=Timmermann|first2=B. N.|last3=Zhang|first3=H.|last4=Gollapudi|first4=R.|last5=Corbett|first5=S.|last6=Samadi|first6=A.|last7=Cohen|first7=M.|title=Wild tomatillos (Physalis species) as food and medicine|journal=Planta Medica|date=2012|volume=78 | issue = 11 |page=IL32|doi=10.1055/s-0032-1320219}} The tomatillo flavor is used in [[fusion cuisine]]s for blending flavors from Latin American dishes with those of Europe and North America.{{cite journal|last1=McGorrin|first1=R. J.|last2=Gimelfarb|first2=L.|title=Comparison of flavor components in fresh and cooked tomatillo with red plum tomato|journal=Developments in Food Science|date=1998|volume=40|pages=295–313|doi=10.1016/S0167-4501(98)80055-1|isbn=9780444825902}} == Botany == === Description === ''P. ixocarpa'' is often confused with ''P. philadelphica'' due to morphological similarities and the fact that neither species have had a clear [[Type (biology)#In botany|type designation]]. ''Physalis ixocarpa'' and ''Physalis philadelphica'' have blue anthers that twist after opening, a yellow corolla with five blue-tinged spots or smudges, and a 10-ribbed calyx filled or burst by the berry. The two species differ in flower size and stigma type.{{Cite journal |last1=Pretz |first1=Chelsea |last2=Deanna |first2=Rocío |date=February 2020 |title=Typifications and nomenclatural notes in Physalis (Solanaceae) from the United States |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/tax.12159 |journal=Taxon |language=en |volume=69 |issue=1 |pages=170–192 |doi=10.1002/tax.12159 |s2cid=214125933 |issn=0040-0262|url-access=subscription }} ''P. philadelphica'' grow up to {{convert|15|to|60|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} and have few hairs on the stem. The leaves have acute and irregularly separated dents on the side.{{Cite book|title=Neglected Crops, 1492 from a Different Perspective.|last1=Montes Hernández|first1=S|last2=Aguirre Rivera|first2=J. R.|publisher=FAO|year=1994|editor-last=Hernándo Bermejo|editor-first=J. E.|volume=26|location=Rome|pages=117–122|chapter=Plant Production and Protection Series|journal=Plant Production and Protection Series|issn=0259-2525|editor-last2=León|editor-first2=J.|chapter-url=http://www.fao.org/docrep/t0646e/T0646E0d.htm|access-date=2017-11-28|archive-date=2014-10-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141011015044/http://www.fao.org/docrep/t0646e/T0646E0d.htm|url-status=dead}} They are typically about {{convert|1|m|ft|0|sp=us|spell=in}} in height, and can be either compact and upright or [[Prostrate shrub|prostrate]] with a wider, less dense canopy. The leaves are typically serrated and can be either smooth or [[Pubescent (botany)|pubescent]]. === Classification === The tomatillo is a member of the genus ''[[Physalis]]'', classified by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753. [[Jean-Baptiste Lamarck|Jean-Baptiste de Lamarck]] described the tomatillo under the name ''Physlis philadelphica'' in 1786. Other species, such as ''P. aeuata'' and ''P. violacea'' were described later. The tomatillo is also often classified as ''P. ixocarpa'' [[Félix Avelar Brotero|Brot]].{{Cite journal|last1=Bukun|first1=Bekir|last2=Uygur|first2=F. Nezihi|last3=Uygur|first3=Sibel|last4=Turkmen|first4=Necattin|last5=Duzenli|first5=Atabay|date=2014-05-16|title=A New Record for the Flora of Turkey: Physalis philadelphica Lam. var. immaculata Waterf. (Solanaceae)|url=http://dergipark.gov.tr/tbtkbotany/issue/11837/141413|journal=Turkish Journal of Botany|language=tr|publication-date=2002|volume=26|issue=5|pages=405–407|issn=1300-008X}} However, ''P. philadelphica'' is the most important species economically.{{Cite book|title=Plant Protoplasts and Genetic Engineering VI|last1=Simpson|first1=J.|last2=Montes-Hernandez|first2=S.|last3=Gutierrez-Campos|first3=R.|last4=Assad-Garcia|first4=N.|last5=Herrera-Estrella|first5=L.|chapter=Genetic Transformation in Physalis Species (Tomatillo) |date=1995|publisher=Springer, Berlin, Heidelberg|isbn=9783642633744|series=Biotechnology in Agriculture and Forestry|volume=34 |pages=228–239|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-3-642-57840-3_21}} The nomenclature for ''Physalis'' has changed since the 1950s. ''P. philadelphica'' was at one time classified as a variety of ''P. ixocarpa''. Later, the classification of ''P. ixocarpa'' was revised under the species of ''P. philadelphica''. Today, the name ''P. ixocarpa'' is commonly used for the domestic plant and ''P. philadelphica'' for the wild one.{{citation needed|date = August 2022}} [[File:Tomatillo plant.jpg|thumb|283x283px|Tomatillo plant with buds, pubescent stem and serrated leaves noticeable]] === Flower === Flowers come in several colors: white, light green, bright yellow, and sometimes purple. Flowers may or may not have purple spots toward the center of the [[Petal|corolla]]. The [[anthers]] are typically dark purple to pale blue. Tomatillo plants are highly [[Self-incompatibility in plants|self-incompatible]], and two or more plants are needed for proper [[pollination]]. Thus, isolated tomatillo plants rarely set fruit.{{cite book|title=Self-Incompatibility in Flowering Plants: Evolution, Diversity and Mechanisms|publisher=Springer|year=2008|isbn=978-3-540-68485-5|editor=Franklin-Tong|editor-first=Vernonica E.|editor-link=Vernonica Franklin-Tong}} === Fruit === The tomatillo fruit is surrounded by an inedible, paper-like [[husk]] formed from the [[sepal|calyx.]] As the fruit matures, it fills the husk and can split it open by harvest time. The husk turns brown, and the fruit can be ripe in several colors, including yellow, green, or even purple. The freshness and greenness of the husk are quality criteria.
'''Flower types:'''
Tomatillo flower white and purple.jpg Tomatillo flower.jpg Starting Tomatillo Verde Flower after pollination maarten smit smitworks.jpg Honeybee and tomatillo flowers.jpg Tomatillo yellow flower.jpg Happy Quinta Feira !!!!! ♥ Physalis philadelphica (8119933598).jpg === Varieties === There are several varieties of tomatillos, with differences in tastes, traits, and ripening colors.{{cite web|title=Tomato and tomatillo varieties|url=https://www.uidaho.edu/-/media/UIdaho-Responsive/Files/Extension/county/twin-falls/Tomatoes-Tomatillos.ashx?la=en&hash=B0D1083C60D6452117A3627D52E56EB4A1B33CE7|publisher=University of Idaho Extension|access-date=29 January 2018}}{{cite web|author1=D.N. Moriconi|author2=M.C. Rush|author3=H. Flores|title=Tomatillo: A Potential Vegetable Crop for Louisiana; In: J. Janick and J.E. Simon (eds.), Advances in new crops|url=https://hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/proceedings1990/V1-407.html|publisher=Timber Press and New Crop Resource Online Program, Center for New Crops & Plant Products, Purdue University.|access-date=29 January 2018|pages=407–413|date=1990}} Some [[cultivar]]s include Amarylla, Chupon, Gigante, Green Husk, Mexican, Pineapple, Purple de Milpa, Rio Grande Verde, and Yellow. === Genetic === ==== Self-incompatibility trait ==== Although self-compatibility is common among wild populations, tomatillos carry [[Self-incompatibility|self-incompatible]] traits. The plant, i.e., the fertile [[hermaphrodite]], is not able to produce zygotes after [[self-pollination]] occurs.{{Cite journal|last1=Mulato-Brito|first1=Juan|last2=Peña-Lomelí|first2=Aureliano|last3=Sahagún-Castellanos|first3=Jaime|last4=Villanueva-Verduzco|first4=Clemente|last5=López-Reynoso|first5=José de Jesús|date=2007-01-01|title=Self-Compatibility Inheritance in Tomatillo (Physalis Ixocarpa Brot.)|journal=Vegetable Crops Research Bulletin|language=en|volume=67|issue=–1|pages=17–24|doi=10.2478/v10032-007-0026-4|issn=1898-7761|doi-access=free}} This limits the ability to improve tomatillo production regarding the seed quality and the production of varieties. The self-compatibility gene is situated in the [[chromosome]]s of the tomatillo and is not inherited through [[cytoplasm]]. Only [[heterozygous]] plants can be self-compatible as the trait is controlled by a [[Dominance (genetics)|dominant gene]]. Tomatillo can thus produce seeds through [[self-pollination]] due to the involvement of self-compatibility traits, but the germination viability is different throughout the produced seeds. This suggests that not only incompatible pollen is involved but also inviability at the seedling stage. A study in 2022 using a commercial cultivar found that it was self-compatible and demonstrated incompatibility only in some of the inter-specific hybrid pollinations that were attempted.{{Cite journal |last1=Junior |first1=André Dutra Silva |last2=Zeist |first2=André Ricardo |last3=da Silva |first3=Daniel Fernandes |last4=de Souza Leal |first4=Murilo Henrique |last5=Oliveira |first5=Guilherme José Almeida |last6=de Oliveira |first6=Joana Nascimento Merces |last7=Youssef |first7=Khamis |last8=Da Rocha Toroco |first8=Bruno |date=2022-05-18 |title=Reproductive biology and hybridization of Physalis L. species |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s40415-022-00811-6 |journal=Brazilian Journal of Botany |volume=45 |issue=3 |pages=1037–1045 |language=en |doi=10.1007/s40415-022-00811-6 |bibcode=2022BrJBo..45.1037J |s2cid=248902866 |issn=1806-9959|url-access=subscription }} == Diseases == Tomatillo is generally a resistant crop as long as its climatic requirements are met. However, as with all crops, mass production brings exposure to pests and diseases. As of 2017, two diseases affecting tomatillos have been documented, namely [[tomato yellow leaf curl virus]] and [[turnip mosaic virus]]. Symptoms of tomato yellow leaf curl virus, including chlorotic margins and [[interveinal]] yellowing, were found in several tomato and tomatillo crops in Mexico and Guatemala in 2006.{{Cite journal|last1=Salati|first1=R.|last2=Shorey|first2=M.|last3=Briggs|first3=A.|last4=Calderon|first4=J.|last5=Rojas|first5=M. R.|last6=Chen|first6=L. F.|last7=Gilbertson|first7=R. L.|last8=Palmieri|first8=M.|date=2010-03-04|title=First Report of Tomato yellow leaf curl virus Infecting Tomato, Tomatillo, and Peppers in Guatemala|journal=Plant Disease|volume=94|issue=4|pages=482|doi=10.1094/PDIS-94-4-0482C|pmid=30754504|issn=0191-2917|doi-access=}} After laboratory tests, the virus was confirmed. Symptomatic plants were associated with the presence of [[Whitefly|whiteflies]], which were likely the cause of this outbreak. Turnip mosaic virus was discovered in several tomatillo crops in California in 2011, rendering 2% of commercially grown tomatillo plants unmarketable, with severe stunting and leaf distortion.{{Cite journal|last1=Liu|first1=H.-Y.|last2=Koike|first2=S. T.|last3=Xu|first3=D.|last4=Li|first4=R.|date=2011-11-02|title=First Report of Turnip mosaic virus in Tomatillo (Physalis philadelphica) in California|journal=Plant Disease|volume=96|issue=2|pages=296|doi=10.1094/PDIS-09-11-0751|pmid=30731815|issn=0191-2917|doi-access=}} The [[Myzus persicae|green peach aphid]] is a common pest in California, and since it readily transmits the turnip mosaic virus, this could be a threat to tomatillo production in California. == See also == {{portal|Food}} * ''[[Physalis peruviana]]'' * [[Salsa (sauce)]] == References == {{Reflist|30em}} == External links == {{Commons category|Physalis philadelphica}} * [http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?7625,7666,7675 Jepson Manual Treatment] * [http://www.plantnames.unimelb.edu.au/Sorting/Physalis.html ''Physalis'' names] * [https://www.nytimes.com/2017/01/09/science/tomatillo-fossils-nightshade.html "Tomatillo Fossils, 52 Million Years Old, Are Discovered in Patagonia"], [[New York Times]], January 9, 2017 {{Taxonbar|from=Q622525}} [[Category:Physalis]] [[Category:Edible Solanaceae]] [[Category:Fruit vegetables]] [[Category:Crops originating from Mexico]] [[Category:Crops originating from Pre-Columbian North America]] [[Category:Berries]] [[Category:Mexican cuisine]] [[Category:Plants described in 1786]] [[Category:Taxa named by Jean-Baptiste Lamarck]] [[Category:Crops originating from indigenous Americans]]
